stories.bridge: That hobby post became the kernel under your phone, the cloud, and this course's labs. Now let's learn to drive it — from the shell up to RHCSA.

figures.name: Andrew Tanenbaum
figures.role: Author of Minix, the system Linux was modeled on

figures.name: Richard Stallman
figures.role: Founder of the GNU project and the Free Software Foundation

stories.hook: On August 25, 1991, a 21-year-old student in Helsinki posted a message to a Usenet group: he was building a free operating system, 'just a hobby.'
stories.narrative: Linus Torvalds was a computer science student at the University of Helsinki who wanted a Unix he could run on his own PC — a 386, the new 32-bit chip. The teaching system Minix, written by Andrew Tanenbaum and published with his 1987 operating-systems textbook, was close to what he wanted, but its license forbade modification and redistribution, and Torvalds kept hitting its limits. So, through the spring and summer of 1991, he started writing his own kernel, borrowing Minix's design as a scaffold while he learned. His August post to comp.os.minix was modest to the point of comedy: he was doing a free operating system, it wouldn't be big or professional like GNU, he'd like feedback on what people wanted. Version 0.01 followed in September — barely functional, a few thousand lines, but real, and it could already run a shell. The decisive move came in 1992, when Torvalds relicensed the kernel under the GNU General Public License. That fused his kernel with Richard Stallman's GNU project, which since 1983 had been building every part of a free Unix — the compiler, the shell, the utilities — except the kernel. GNU plus Linux was a complete operating system, and the early internet did the rest: thousands of contributors, mailing lists, a development model nobody had planned and everybody copied. Linux 1.0 was declared in March 1994. The famous Tanenbaum-Torvalds debate of 1992 — monolithic versus microkernel design, argued fiercely on Usenet — ended with history siding, messily, with Torvalds. He never got rich from Linux and never controlled it; what he built was infrastructure. Today Linux runs the world's supercomputers, most of the cloud, and — via Android — most of the world's phones. The hobby outgrew every professional plan, and this module teaches you to administer what it became.
stories.title: The story behind Linux
verifiedClaims: Torvalds announced Linux on comp.os.minix on August 25, 1991, calling it 'just a hobby'
Minix was published by Tanenbaum in 1987 with a restrictive license
Stallman launched the GNU project in 1983

stories.bridge: A memo about sharing a printer became the wiring standard of civilization. Now let's learn the protocols that still speak Metcalfe's language — starting with the frame.
stories.hook: On May 22, 1973, Bob Metcalfe wrote a memo at Xerox PARC describing a network for the Alto computer. He called it Ethernet.
stories.narrative: Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center had built the Alto — the first personal computer with a graphical interface, the machine that taught Steve Jobs what a computer could be — and now the Altos needed to share an expensive laser printer. Metcalfe, with David Boggs, designed a system inspired by the ALOHAnet, a radio network linking the Hawaiian islands: stations would listen before transmitting, and if two talked at once, both would back off for a random interval and retry. The name came from the old physics concept of the 'luminiferous ether,' the medium once thought to carry light — Metcalfe's joke was that his network carried bits through the ether. The first experimental Ethernet ran on November 11, 1973, at 2.94 megabits per second over coaxial cable. Metcalfe left Xerox and founded 3Com in 1979 to commercialize it; the DIX consortium (Digital, Intel, Xerox) published a standard in 1980, and the IEEE blessed it as 802.3 in 1983. Ethernet then did something unusual in technology: it won slowly and completely, absorbing every rival — Token Ring, FDDI, ATM — by being cheap, simple, and good enough to keep improving, from 10 megabits to 400 gigabits and beyond. Metcalfe also gave the industry its favorite network adage, Metcalfe's law: a network's value grows with the square of its users — the reason every network in this module gets more useful the more you connect to it. Every wired port you will configure in this course, from a home switch to a data-center fabric, is a descendant of that 1973 memo about a printer. The "ether" in Ethernet was itself a joke about dead physics — the luminiferous ether had been disproven decades earlier, but Metcalfe liked the image of bits radiating through a common medium. The medium changed from coaxial cable to twisted pair to fiber, the speed from 3 megabits to 400 gigabits, but the frame format's bones are still 1973. Learn the frame and you can read any of it.
stories.title: The story behind Ethernet
verifiedClaims: Metcalfe's Ethernet memo is dated May 22, 1973
The first experimental network ran November 11, 1973
Metcalfe founded 3Com in 1979; IEEE standardized Ethernet as 802.3 in 1983

stories.bridge: Two letters, one crash, and the network survived — that resilience was the whole point. Now let's learn the protocols that grew from that night, layer by layer.

figures.name: Leonard Kleinrock
figures.role: UCLA professor; ARPANET pioneer whose lab sent the first message

figures.name: Paul Baran
figures.role: RAND researcher; developed distributed packet-switching concepts 1960–1964

stories.hook: At 10:30 PM on October 29, 1969, a UCLA student typed the letters L and O — and the network crashed.
stories.narrative: Charley Kline sat at a terminal in Leonard Kleinrock's laboratory at UCLA, connected to a refrigerator-sized Interface Message Processor — the first node of the ARPANET, installed that September. On the other end, at the Stanford Research Institute some 350 miles north, a colleague waited by a phone. The plan was to log in remotely: Kline would type L-O-G-I-N, confirming each letter by phone as the characters traveled the new network. He typed L. 'Got the L,' came the reply. He typed O. 'Got the O.' Then the SRI machine crashed under the load — its memory filled, the system went down. The first message ever sent on the ancestor of the internet was 'LO' — as in, lo and behold. An hour later they tried again and it worked, but history kept the crash. The ideas behind that night had been brewing for a decade: Paul Baran at RAND, writing memoranda between 1960 and 1964, had shown that a communications network built from small chopped-up messages, routed dynamically with no center, could survive nuclear attack; Donald Davies at Britain's National Physical Laboratory had independently invented the same technique and, in 1965–66, gave it its immortal name — the packet. Kleinrock himself had supplied the mathematics, a 1962 MIT doctoral thesis on message delay in networks that made the whole thing analyzable. By December 1969 four sites were connected — UCLA, SRI, UC Santa Barbara, and Utah — and the crash-prone experiment began its fifty-year run to ubiquity. The lesson of 'LO' is the one this module keeps teaching: the network was designed to survive failure, not to avoid it. Packets route around damage. So should your designs. Kleinrock kept the lab notebooks, and the IMP log for that night survives — "talked to SRI host to host" scrawled in the margin of history. Within two years the network had email; within a decade, TCP/IP; within a quarter century, the web. Every protocol you'll configure in this module is a refinement of the bet those four nodes made: that a network which expects failure will outlive one that pretends it won't happen.
stories.title: The story behind the first message on the internet
verifiedClaims: The first ARPANET message was sent October 29, 1969, from UCLA to SRI; the system crashed after 'LO' of 'LOGIN'
Baran's RAND memoranda on distributed communications date to 1960–1964
Davies coined 'packet' in 1965–1966; Kleinrock's doctoral thesis was 1962
